items.t: Inflammatory and autoimmune disease (rheumatic and collagen disease, severe allergy including asthma and anaphylaxis), adrenocortical insufficiency, cerebral oedema (not from head injury), lymphocytic leukaemia, anti-emetic with chemotherapy, palliative care; Cushing's suppression tests (one UK SmPC); COVID-19 needing oxygen (adults and adolescents 12 years and over, at least 40 kg).

src.q: Dexamethasone Oral Solution is used for the treatment of various inflammatory and autoimmune diseases
adjunct in the control of cerebral oedema (not in those cases where the oedema is caused by head injury)

Dexamethasone is indicated in the treatment of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in adult and adolescent patients (aged 12 years and older with body weight at least 40 kg) who require supplemental oxygen therapy.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK 2 mg/5 mL oral solution SmPCs or SPS pages accessed.

items.t: Adults: usual dose 0.5-10 mg daily (another UK SmPC: initial 0.5-9 mg daily, higher in severe disease). Use the lowest effective dose; preferably in the morning. Chronic dosing should preferably not exceed 1.5 mg daily.

src.q: The usual dose in adults is 0.5-10 mg per day.
The initial dosage varies from 0.5 - 9mg a day depending on the disease being treated.
Chronic dosage should preferably not exceed 1.5mg dexamethasone daily.

items.t: Acute self-limiting allergic disorders (one UK SmPC): after an injection on day 1, 1 mg twice daily on days 2-3, 500 micrograms twice daily on days 4-5, 500 micrograms daily on days 6-7, reassess on day 8.

src.q: Second day: 1mg (2.5ml) Dexamethasone Oral Solution twice a day.
Eighth day: Re-assessment.

items.t: Recurrent or inoperable brain tumour (palliative, maintenance): 2 mg two or three times a day may be effective; use the smallest dose that controls symptoms.

src.q: A dosage of 2mg two or three times a day may be effective.

items.t: COVID-19 needing oxygen: 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days (adults; adolescents 12 years and over).

src.q: For the treatment of Covid-19 Adult patients 6 mg PO once a day for up to 10 days.

items.t: Withdrawal: after more than 3 weeks, do not stop abruptly; slow the taper once about 1 mg daily is reached. Up to about 6 mg daily for 3 weeks is unlikely to cause relevant HPA suppression, except in at-risk groups.

src.q: In patients who have received dexamethasone for more than 3 weeks, withdrawal should not be abrupt.
Once a daily dose of approx. 1 mg dexamethasone is reached, dose reduction should be slower to allow the HPA-axis to recover.
Abrupt withdrawal of doses up to approx. 6 mg dexamethasone for 3 weeks is unlikely to lead to clinically relevant HPA-axis suppression, in the majority of patients.

items.t: Elderly, renal or hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Elderly, renal impairment, hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is needed.

items.t: Use in children only with caution (growth retardation); dose set individually by the physician. One UK SmPC: limit to a single dose on alternate days to lessen growth retardation and adrenal suppression.

src.q: Dexamethasone should only be administered to children with caution, since glucocorticoids can induce growth retardation. The daily dose should be determined by the physician for each child individually.
Dosage should be limited to a single dose on alternate days to lessen retardation of growth and minimize suppression of hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis.

items.t: Childhood croup (one UK SmPC): single dose 0.15 mg/kg; a second dose may be given after 12 hours if needed; maximum 10 mg.

src.q: Childhood Croup: A single dose of 0.15mg/kg Dexamethasone Oral Solution is recommended. A second dose may be administered after 12 hours, if considered necessary by the treating physician.
However, a maximum dose of 10mg (25ml Dexsol Oral Solution) is recommended.

items.t: COVID-19, adolescents 12 years and over (at least 40 kg): 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days.

src.q: Paediatric patients (adolescents aged 12 years and older with body weight at least 40kg) are recommended to take 6mg orally, once a day for up to 10 days.

items.t: Excipients (both UK solutions): propylene glycol (serious effects possible under 5 years with alcohol dehydrogenase substrates such as ethanol) and benzoic acid (may increase jaundice in newborns).

src.q: Co-administration with any substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase such as ethanol may induce serious adverse effects in children less than 5 years old.
Benzoic acid may increase jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) in newborn babies (up to 4 weeks old).

items.t: Both UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity; gastric or duodenal ulcer; systemic fungal infection; parasitic/tropical worm infection.

src.q: Systemic fungal infections. - Stomach ulcer or duodenal ulcer - Infection with tropical worms - Parasitic infection
gastric and duodenal ulcer; acute infections: viral infections and systemic fungal infections

items.t: One UK SmPC: acute viral infections; vaccination with live vaccines. Another UK SmPC: systemic infection unless specific anti-infective therapy is given; avoid live vaccines at immunosuppressive doses; contraindications generally do not apply when glucocorticoids may be life-saving.

Systemic infection unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed.

items.t: Particular care and frequent monitoring in: osteoporosis, hypertension or heart failure, diabetes (or family history), tuberculosis history, glaucoma (or family history), previous steroid myopathy, liver failure, renal insufficiency, epilepsy, peptic ulceration; one UK SmPC adds myasthenia gravis, hypothyroidism, migraine, herpes simplex, ulcerative colitis/diverticulitis/fresh anastomosis. Great caution after recent myocardial infarction.

src.q: Particular care is required when considering the use of systemic glucocorticoids in patients with the following conditions and frequent patient monitoring is necessary
myasthenia gravis - non-specific ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis or fresh intestinal anastomosis - peptic ulceration - liver failure - renal insufficiency - hypothyroidism - epilepsy - migraine
corticosteroids should be used with great caution in these patients

items.t: Severe psychiatric reactions may occur, usually within days or weeks; particular care with personal or first-degree family history of severe affective disorder or steroid psychosis.

src.q: Patient/carers should be encouraged to seek medical advice if worrying psychological symptoms develop, especially if depressed mood or suicidal ideation is suspected.
These would include depressive or manic-depressive illness and previous steroid psychosis.

items.t: Infections may be masked; chickenpox and measles can be fatal in immunosuppressed patients (non-immune exposed patients need VZIG within 10 days). Rule out latent amoebiasis or strongyloidiasis in people from the tropics or with unexplained diarrhoea.

src.q: Chickenpox is a normally minor illness but may be fatal in immunosuppressed patients
It is recommended that these are ruled out before initiating corticosteroid therapy particularly in those patients who have spent time in the tropics or those with unexplained diarrhoea.

items.t: Phaeochromocytoma: crisis can be fatal; use only after risk/benefit evaluation. Tumour lysis syndrome in haematological malignancy: monitor high-risk patients.

src.q: Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma after an appropriate risk/benefit evaluation
Patients at high risk of TLS such as patients with high proliferative rate, high tumour burden, and high sensitivity to cytotoxic agents, should be monitored closely

items.t: Blurred vision: consider ophthalmology referral. Hypokalaemia should be corrected before starting (one UK SmPC).

src.q: the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of possible causes
Hypokalemia should be corrected before corticosteroid treatment initiation.

items.t: Excipients: both UK oral solutions contain sorbitol and maltitol; people with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take them.

items.t: CYP3A inhibitors (including cobicistat; e.g. ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin, macrolides): raise dexamethasone levels; avoid unless benefit outweighs risk, and monitor.

src.q: The combination should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid side-effects.
Macrolide antibiotics have been reported to cause a significant decrease in corticosteroid clearance

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, rifampicin, rifabutin, ephedrine): lower dexamethasone levels; dose may need increasing. Dexamethasone itself is a moderate CYP3A4 inducer and may lower levels of CYP3A4 substrates.

src.q: may lead to decreased plasma concentrations of dexamethasone and the dose may need to be increased
Dexamethasone is a moderate inducer of CYP 3A4.

items.t: NSAIDs: more peptic ulceration; monitor. Salicylates: steroids increase salicylate clearance; reduce salicylate dose as the steroid is withdrawn; caution with aspirin in hypoprothrombinaemia.

src.q: Patients taking NSAID's should be monitored since the incidence and/or severity of gastro-ulceration may increase.
The renal clearance of salicylates is increased by corticosteroids and therefore, salicylate dosage should be reduced along with steroidal withdrawal.

items.t: Oral anticoagulants (coumarins): effect may change; bleeding risk at high doses or over 10 days; monitor INR closely (one UK SmPC: check on day 8 then every 2 weeks during and after treatment).

biological investigations on 8th day, then every 2 weeks during treatment and after treatment discontinuation

src.q: Concurrent use of potassium-depleting diuretics (e.g. acetazolamide, loop diuretics, thiazide diuretics or carbenoxolone) and glucocorticoids may result in severe hypokalaemia.
